name: Mockuuups Bento Grid Examples
tagline: Listicle of 9 named sites using bento-grid layouts, with a short read on each
description: A content-marketing blog post on Mockuuups Studio's site (a 5,300-scene device mockup generator for macOS, Windows and Linux) that explains what a bento grid is and walks through nine real-world uses of the pattern. Written by David Stefanides, first published 22 February 2024 and re-titled for 2026. The named examples are Literal, Create.video, Apple.com, Halcyon Logistics, Iconwerk, Procreate, Lottie Lessons by 10xDesigners, Koto Studio's WhatsApp case study, and Bento. It is a reference for the layout pattern, not a code resource — no markup, tokens or components are provided.
agent_guidance: Use this only as a naming source when a user says 'bento grid' and you need concrete sites to describe the pattern back to them — Apple.com and Procreate are the two worth citing. It gives you zero code, so pair it with an actual grid implementation (CSS grid with named areas, or a shadcn-style bento block) and do not expect responsive breakpoints or spacing tokens from here. The value is in the example list; the surrounding prose is 2024 SEO copy refreshed with a 2026 date.
why_it_matters: Bento grids are now the default marketing-page layout, and this is one of the few pages that names specific production examples rather than showing anonymous dribbble shots.

name: Kling AI Review — Max Productive
tagline: Affiliate directory review of Kling AI with renewal-price and support warnings
description: A long review page on max-productive.ai, an affiliate-monetised AI tools directory. It rates Kling AI 4.5 stars, cites a 1243 ELO benchmark score, and is unusually blunt about the downsides: introductory $6.99/mo Standard renewing at $8.80/mo, customer support described as effectively non-existent, credits deducted for failed generations, and content censorship under Chinese regulations. A comparison table sets it against Runway ($15/mo), Pika ($28/mo commercial) and Luma AI ($29.99/mo commercial). There is no author byline and no independently captured screenshots, so the firsthand-testing claims cannot be verified.
pricing_detail: Quotes Kling Standard at $6.99/mo introductory renewing at $8.80/mo; competitor table lists Runway $15/mo, Pika $28/mo commercial, Luma AI $29.99/mo commercial.
agent_guidance: Treat this as one weak signal, never as a price source — it is an affiliate page with no byline, so cross-check every number against Kling's own billing page or the CostBench entry in this index before repeating it to a user. The one genuinely useful thing here is the intro-versus-renewal pricing warning and the 'credits burn on failed generations' note, which vendor pages omit. Do not cite the ELO figure as fact.
why_it_matters: Documents the intro-price bait and credit-burn behaviour of Kling that vendor and agency content marketing consistently leaves out.
evidence: https://max-productive.ai/ai-tools/kling-ai (fetched twice, second pass with a skeptical extraction prompt)

name: Kling 3.0 Guide — invideo
tagline: Feature and prompting guide for Kling 3.0 multi-shot video, from invideo's blog
description: A vendor-published guide from invideo.io explaining Kling 3.0 as a scene-aware AI director that produces 3–15 second multi-shot clips from structured prompts, with camera control, character consistency, native audio and on-frame text. It compares 3.0 against Kling 2.6 and Kling O1, covers credit-based pricing, and ends with prompting and workflow tips plus a fit assessment for production stacks. invideo bundles Kling inside its own editing, branding and music suite, so the framing is promotional — the feature and prompting detail is still the most structured writeup of the model's shot-level controls.
pricing_detail: Free tier ~66 credits/day; standard plans $10–$15/mo for ~660 credits; pro tiers $35–$40/mo for ~3,000 credits (a ~$32.56/mo Pro plan is cited as roughly 6 min of 720p or 4 min of 1080p per month).
agent_guidance: Reach for this when a user needs to write Kling prompts, not when they need to choose a model — the prompting and camera-control sections are the payload, and the comparison against Kling 2.6 and O1 is the fastest way to know which version's syntax you are targeting. Discount the pricing numbers and the 'right for your stack' verdict: invideo resells Kling access, so the conclusion is always going to be yes. Pair it with the CostBench entry for real tier prices.
why_it_matters: One of the few writeups that treats Kling as a shot-level director with structured prompt syntax rather than a text-to-video toy, which is what actually matters when scripting it.

name: Kling AI Pricing — CostBench
tagline: Full Kling tier table plus 11 documented hidden costs and a median contract figure
description: CostBench is a SaaS pricing-intelligence site that tracks list prices, hidden costs and real contract values across software categories. Its Kling page gives the complete tier table — Free (66 credits/day, 5s clips), Standard $6.99/mo or $6.60 annual (660 credits), Pro $25.99/$24.42 (3,000), Premier $64.99/$60.72 (8,000), Ultra $180/$119.16 (26,000) — and then enumerates 11 hidden costs including monthly credit expiry with no rollover, forfeited credits on plan switches, auto-renewal charges after cancellation, a ~3x credit surcharge for the newer model, and 1–2 day queue delays. It reports a median actual contract of $293/year across five verified purchases.
pricing_detail: Kling tiers: Free (66 credits/day, 5s); Standard $6.99/mo, $6.60/mo annual, 660 credits, 10s; Pro $25.99/mo, $24.42 annual, 3,000 credits; Premier $64.99/mo, $60.72 annual, 8,000 credits; Ultra $180/mo, $119.16 annual, 26,000 credits. Median verified contract $293/year (n=5).
agent_guidance: This is the pricing source to trust in this batch — when a user asks what Kling costs or budgets a generation pipeline, quote these tiers rather than the invideo or Max Productive numbers, and warn them that credits expire monthly and are forfeited on plan switches, which wrecks naive per-clip cost math. Use the credits-per-tier column to size a plan against expected clip volume, and remember the newer model burns ~3x credits per generation. Re-verify before quoting: it is a third-party tracker, not Kling's billing page.
why_it_matters: Credit-based AI video pricing is deliberately hard to compare, and this is a structured tier table with the expiry and forfeiture traps written down.

name: remove.bg Review — SaaSCRMReview
tagline: Affiliate review of remove.bg with credit-tier prices and a hair-detail failure list
description: A 16-section affiliate review of remove.bg on SaaSCRMReview, a solo-run software review site (byline 'Macedona') claiming 175+ published reviews. It lists annual-billing credit tiers — Lite $8.10/mo for up to 40 credits, Pro $35.10/mo for 200, Volume+ $80.10/mo for 500, plus a free tier of roughly 50 watermarked preview-resolution images — scores cutout accuracy 8.5/10, and states a 200+ image test with 88% clean edges on 50 product photos and ~60% flyaway hair retained versus manual masking. Verdict: yes for ecommerce and teams over 50 images a month, no for one-off cutouts. The numbers are self-reported with no published sample images, and a 'Key Entities & Concepts' section marks it as SEO-shaped content.
pricing_detail: remove.bg annual billing as listed: Lite $8.10/mo ($97.20/yr, up to 40 credits/mo); Pro $35.10/mo ($421.20/yr, 200 credits/mo); Volume+ $80.10/mo ($961.20/yr, 500 credits/mo). Free tier ~50 images/mo, watermarked and low resolution.
agent_guidance: Use this only for the failure-mode list — fine hair, glass and plastic transparency, and low-contrast backgrounds are where remove.bg breaks, which is worth telling a user before they buy credits for a portrait or jewellery catalogue. Do not quote its prices without checking remove.bg directly; the tiers are credit-based and change, and this page is affiliate-monetised with a single unnamed reviewer and no sample outputs. For a design pipeline, the API and Photoshop plugin are the parts that matter, and this covers both briefly.
why_it_matters: Names the specific image classes where automated background removal fails, which is the one thing a vendor page will never tell you before you spend credits.
evidence: https://saascrmreview.com/remove-bg-review (fetched twice, second pass with a skeptical extraction prompt)
